## Biopython · Install + Theory {.smaller}

[Biopython · setup]{.eyebrow}

### The plumbing: read every format, draw on matplotlib

```bash
pip install biopython
```

```{.python}
from io import StringIO                                         # read newick from a string
from Bio import Phylo, SeqIO                                    # tree IO + record IO
from Bio.Graphics import GenomeDiagram                          # circular + linear maps
from Bio.SeqRecord import SeqRecord                             # holds a sequence + features
from Bio.Seq import Seq                                         # the sequence itself
from Bio.SeqFeature import SeqFeature, SimpleLocation           # gene / CDS features
```

**Theory.** Biopython is the **plumbing of bioinformatics**: it reads/writes
**every common format** (Newick, Nexus, PhyloXML, FASTA, GenBank, EMBL …) and
exposes the result as plain Python objects.

- **`Bio.Phylo`** — tree IO + a matplotlib `draw()` that lays out the tree on a
  normal `Axes`. Stack it above a heatmap, side-by-side with a Manhattan plot,
  anywhere you'd put any other matplotlib panel.
- **`Bio.Graphics.GenomeDiagram`** — high-level builder for **publication-quality
  plasmid maps** (circular) and **linear gene tracks** with arrow sigils. Renders
  to PNG/SVG/PDF directly; no matplotlib needed under the hood.

## Biopython · The Data {.smaller}

[Biopython · data peek]{.eyebrow}

### Same 9-tip Newick, parsed by Phylo + ASCII preview

We reuse the Newick string from the Toytree section. `Phylo.read(StringIO(...))`
returns a `Tree` object; `Phylo.draw_ascii` prints it as text — useful for log
files and sanity-checking parsing before drawing.

```{python}
#| echo: true
from io import StringIO                                         # treat the string as a file
from Bio import Phylo                                           # tree IO + draw

# same 9-tip phylogeny we used in the Toytree section
newick = "((((A:1.2,B:1.5):2.1,(C:0.9,D:1.7):1.8):3.0," \
         "(E:2.3,F:1.6):2.7):1.5,((G:1.9,H:2.0):2.3,I:3.5):1.4);"

tree = Phylo.read(StringIO(newick), "newick")                   # parse Newick -> Tree
print("terminals:", [t.name for t in tree.get_terminals()])     # leaf names
Phylo.draw_ascii(tree)                                          # text-art preview
```


<!-- slide 80 -->
## Biopython · Step 1 — `Phylo.draw` on Matplotlib {.smaller}

[Biopython · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Draws on the current axes — `None` return value

`Phylo.draw(tree)` does **not** return a figure; it draws onto the **current
matplotlib axes** (or creates one). Create the `Axes` yourself with
`plt.subplots()` so you control the size + can stack the tree with other panels.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7|9-14"}
from io import StringIO                                 # newick from string
from Bio import Phylo                                   # tree IO + draw

newick = "((((A:1.2,B:1.5):2.1,(C:0.9,D:1.7):1.8):3.0," \
         "(E:2.3,F:1.6):2.7):1.5,((G:1.9,H:2.0):2.3,I:3.5):1.4);"
tree = Phylo.read(StringIO(newick), "newick")           # parse once

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))              # CREATE axes for the tree
Phylo.draw(                                             # CALL — draws on `ax`
    tree,
    axes=ax,                                            # explicit axes target
    do_show=False,                                      # don't pop a window
)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)          # match cream style
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
from io import StringIO
from Bio import Phylo

newick = "((((A:1.2,B:1.5):2.1,(C:0.9,D:1.7):1.8):3.0," \
         "(E:2.3,F:1.6):2.7):1.5,((G:1.9,H:2.0):2.3,I:3.5):1.4);"
tree = Phylo.read(StringIO(newick), "newick")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
Phylo.draw(tree, axes=ax, do_show=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```
:::

<!-- slide 81 -->
## Biopython · Step 2 — Colour Branches by Clade {.smaller}

[Biopython · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Walk the tree, set `clade.color`

Bio.Phylo's `Tree` is a recursive structure. Walk it with
`tree.find_clades()`, set `clade.color = "#hex"` on each non-terminal subtree,
and `Phylo.draw` picks up the colours automatically. Below: each top-level
clade in a different Economist hue.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7|9-13|15-19"}
from io import StringIO                                 # newick from string
from Bio import Phylo                                   # tree IO + draw

newick = "((((A:1.2,B:1.5):2.1,(C:0.9,D:1.7):1.8):3.0," \
         "(E:2.3,F:1.6):2.7):1.5,((G:1.9,H:2.0):2.3,I:3.5):1.4);"
tree = Phylo.read(StringIO(newick), "newick")           # parse Tree

# colour the two top-level children of the root in two course hues
palette = [GREEN, BLUE]                                 # one hue per major clade
for clade, colour in zip(tree.root.clades, palette):    # iterate top-level subtrees
    clade.color = colour                                # set hex; Phylo.draw honours it

# CREATE the axes, CALL Phylo.draw — colours come through automatically
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))              # CREATE axes
Phylo.draw(tree, axes=ax, do_show=False)                # CALL — picks up clade.color
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)          # cream style
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
from io import StringIO
from Bio import Phylo

newick = "((((A:1.2,B:1.5):2.1,(C:0.9,D:1.7):1.8):3.0," \
         "(E:2.3,F:1.6):2.7):1.5,((G:1.9,H:2.0):2.3,I:3.5):1.4);"
tree = Phylo.read(StringIO(newick), "newick")

palette = [GREEN, BLUE]
for clade, colour in zip(tree.root.clades, palette):
    clade.color = colour

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
Phylo.draw(tree, axes=ax, do_show=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```
:::

<!-- slide 82 -->
## Biopython · Step 3 — Circular Plasmid Diagram {.smaller}

[Biopython · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · `GenomeDiagram` — five genes on a 5 kb plasmid

`GenomeDiagram` builds publication-quality plasmid maps. The pattern:
1. wrap the sequence in a `SeqRecord`,
2. attach `SeqFeature` objects (gene boxes),
3. create a `Diagram`, add a `Track`, add a `FeatureSet`,
4. `.draw(format="circular", ...)`,
5. `.write(path, "PNG")`.

We embed the resulting PNG with `![](...)`.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-12|14-22|24-31|33-37"}
from pathlib import Path                                # cross-platform paths
from Bio.SeqRecord import SeqRecord; from Bio.Seq import Seq
from Bio.SeqFeature import SeqFeature, SimpleLocation
from Bio.Graphics import GenomeDiagram                  # the diagram builder

# 5 kb dummy plasmid backbone + 5 gene features
record = SeqRecord(Seq("N" * 5000), id="plasmid")       # 5000-bp scaffold
gene_spans = [(  50,  900, +1, "geneA", GREEN),         # (start, end, strand, name, hue)
              (1100, 1900, +1, "geneB", BLUE),
              (2200, 3000, -1, "geneC", AMBER),
              (3200, 3900, +1, "geneD", RED),
              (4100, 4900, -1, "geneE", PURPLE)]
for s, e, strand, name, _ in gene_spans:                # build SeqFeature objects
    record.features.append(SeqFeature(
        SimpleLocation(s, e, strand=strand),            # interval + strand
        type="gene", qualifiers={"label": [name]}))     # label shows on diagram

# CREATE — Diagram -> Track -> FeatureSet (three layers)
gd  = GenomeDiagram.Diagram("toy plasmid")              # top-level container
trk = gd.new_track(1, name="genes", greytrack=False,    # one ring track
                   scale_largetick_interval=1000)       # axis tick every 1 kb
fs  = trk.new_set()                                     # features live on this set
for (s, e, strand, name, hue), feat in zip(gene_spans, record.features):
    fs.add_feature(feat, color=hue, label=True,         # paint + label this gene
                   sigil="ARROW", label_size=10,
                   label_angle=0)

# CALL — draw circular + write PNG to disk
out = Path("figures/biopy_plasmid.svg"); out.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
gd.draw(format="circular", circular=True,               # circular layout
        pagesize=(800, 800), start=0, end=5000,         # full extent
        circle_core=0.6)                                # inner radius
gd.write(str(out), "SVG")                               # SVG avoids the rlPyCairo PNG backend

# embed the rendered PNG via markdown
from IPython.display import Image
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(filename=str(out))
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 83 -->
## Biopython · Step 4 — Linear Gene Track {.smaller}

[Biopython · build]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Same features, `format="linear"`, ARROW sigils

Switch `format="circular"` to `"linear"` and the same `Diagram` redraws as a
horizontal gene track. Arrows now point in the strand direction — forward
genes right, reverse genes left. Same data, same colours, different geometry.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="24-31"}
from pathlib import Path                                # cross-platform paths
from Bio.SeqRecord import SeqRecord; from Bio.Seq import Seq
from Bio.SeqFeature import SeqFeature, SimpleLocation
from Bio.Graphics import GenomeDiagram                  # the diagram builder

# same 5 gene features as the circular step
record = SeqRecord(Seq("N" * 5000), id="plasmid")
gene_spans = [(  50,  900, +1, "geneA", GREEN),
              (1100, 1900, +1, "geneB", BLUE),
              (2200, 3000, -1, "geneC", AMBER),
              (3200, 3900, +1, "geneD", RED),
              (4100, 4900, -1, "geneE", PURPLE)]
for s, e, strand, name, _ in gene_spans:
    record.features.append(SeqFeature(
        SimpleLocation(s, e, strand=strand),
        type="gene", qualifiers={"label": [name]}))

gd  = GenomeDiagram.Diagram("toy genome")               # new top-level container
trk = gd.new_track(1, name="genes", greytrack=False,    # one horizontal track
                   scale_largetick_interval=1000)
fs  = trk.new_set()
for (s, e, strand, name, hue), feat in zip(gene_spans, record.features):
    fs.add_feature(feat, color=hue, label=True,
                   sigil="ARROW", label_size=9, label_angle=30,
                   arrowshaft_height=0.7)               # chunky strand arrows

# CALL — linear layout, wider than tall
out = Path("figures/biopy_linear.svg"); out.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
gd.draw(format="linear", orientation="landscape",       # horizontal track
        pagesize=(900, 220), start=0, end=5000,         # full extent
        fragments=1)                                    # one row, no wrap
gd.write(str(out), "SVG")

from IPython.display import Image
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(filename=str(out))
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 84 -->
## Biopython · Takeaway {.smaller}

[Biopython · recap]{.eyebrow}

### The plumbing for trees + feature diagrams

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **`Phylo.read(file, format)`** parses Newick / Nexus / PhyloXML; **`Phylo.draw`**
   lays the tree on any matplotlib `Axes`.
2. **`clade.color = "#hex"`** colours subtrees in-place — `Phylo.draw` picks it up.
3. **`GenomeDiagram`** stacks `Diagram → Track → FeatureSet`; one `Diagram` can
   render circular **and** linear without rebuilding the features.
4. **`sigil="ARROW"`** + strand sign gives canonical gene-track arrows.
5. Output is **PNG / SVG / PDF directly** — no matplotlib needed under the hood.
:::

**Compare with:** pair **`Phylo`** with **Toytree** (section 3) — Phylo for IO,
Toytree for prettier display. Pair **`Bio.Graphics`** with
**`dna_features_viewer`** (section 7) — Bio.Graphics for plasmid-style circular
publication output, dna_features_viewer for matplotlib-native gene maps you can
stack with the rest of your figure. Biopython is the plumbing; the other
libraries are the polish.
